text: A fresh install of Windows Server does almost nothing on its own — it's a blank operating system until an administrator adds roles. In this lesson we'll look at the handful of roles you'll run into constantly in the field: Active Directory Domain Services, DNS, DHCP, File Server, and IIS. Then we'll zero in on the one that matters most for the rest of this chapter — AD DS — and exactly what a domain controller does once you turn it on.

You add roles through the Add Roles and Features Wizard in Server Manager, or faster, from PowerShell. Install-WindowsFeature -Name AD-Domain-Services -IncludeManagementTools installs Active Directory Domain Services along with its management tools, like Active Directory Users and Computers, in a single line — no wizard clicking required once you're standing up more than one server.

AD DS is the identity and authentication backbone of a Windows network. DNS resolves names to IP addresses, and specifically, it's how a workstation finds a domain controller in the first place — AD DS literally cannot function without DNS, which is why they're usually installed together. DHCP hands out IP addresses, gateways, and DNS servers automatically, instead of an administrator typing a static address into every machine by hand. File and Storage Services turns a server into shared storage, the role behind a mapped network drive. And Web Server, or IIS, hosts websites and web applications.

Installing AD DS and promoting a server to a domain controller gives it three concrete jobs. It authenticates logons and issues Kerberos tickets — proof of identity a computer presents to other servers without retyping a password. It hosts SYSVOL, the shared folder holding Group Policy Objects and logon scripts. And it stores the AD database, replicating every change to every other domain controller automatically.

That's what a domain controller is actually doing under the hood. Next, we'll zoom out to the structure those domain controllers belong to — forests, trees, domains, and organizational units — and why OUs exist in the first place.
